[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]Bioshock 2[/b] returns the player to the vividly atmospheric world of [i]Rapture[/i] and reintroduces all of the positive qualities that were prevalent in the first installment of this franchise. It is very, very similar to the first; so expect it to play like a refined continuation rather than an entirely new game. But it does offer a more intimate perspective on the underwater dystopia, as the player will take on the role of a unique [i]Big Daddy[/i] this time around and will be much more connected to the city. Most of the features are extremely similar to their counterparts in the original game; however there was definitely fine-tuning applied to some aspects. Perhaps most prominently, the combat and overall gameplay is significantly more exciting this time around. Overall, it is a great game that was mostly successful in living up to the high standard set by the first game.

Now, it is essentially a direct sequel. Having played both games, I would suggest that you attempt to play the first one before this, if you can afford the time and money. Although, it isn’t entirely necessary and you could opt to read a synopsis rather than play through the entire first game. But I would suggest you at least do that to get a little background information. Doing so will provide you the opportunity to fully enjoy the subtle nuances throughout the game.

As for the specifics, [b]Bioshock 2[/b] is a fundamentally well-crafted game for all the same reasons the original was. At the forefront, there is once again an exceptionally intriguing atmosphere and a wondrous gameworld design. The city of [i]Rapture[/i] continues to fascinate. Throughout your adventure, you will probably notice that all of the subtle niceties and ancillary details add up to create a very immersive and pleasurable experience. I personally feel the ambiance of the gameworld is best quality of this game and holds true to the brand.

The multidirectional storytelling that was expertly executed in the first game also returns in this sequel. The main storyline will unfold as you progress through the campaign, but you also can learn a great deal about the backstory and lore if you explore and if you seek out the collectibles. A lot is left up to the player to determine how much he/she wants to learn about the lore. The narrative elements are mostly well written and enticing; and the foundation of it all is the superbly idiosyncratic NPCs. It all comes together quite nicely. All of that said, the narrative elements as a whole may feel a little less interesting in [b]Bioshock 2[/b] than they were in the first— perhaps due to the unavoidable loss of novelty of core concepts that is intrinsic to all sequels.

As for the actual gameplay, it is significantly more exciting in [b]Bioshock 2[/b] than in the original.  There were nice refinements to the combat system, and the fact you now can maul people with the patented [i]Big Daddy Drill[/i] is an added bonus. But also the actual fight sequences are better designed, and the layout of the combat zones provides more opportunities for creativity and hazard-kills. And new gameplay systems like the harvesting of ADAM from dead [i]splicers[/i] really brings the high-action combat element of the game to the forefront of the overall experience much more than in the first installment.

There is also a multiplayer mode and although it has the potential to be quite fun, it suffers from a low population and not-so-friendly community of regulars. If you have the patience to deal with the wait times and inevitable toxic matches, you will occasionally find yourself in some games that can be pretty enjoyable. But I wouldn’t count on the multiplayer adding too much value to the game; the focus is definitely on the campaign.

In summary, I would say that [b]Bioshock 2[/b] is a very good game, although perhaps not quite as masterful as the original. It is strongly tied to its predecessor, and so it would probably be best to play both if you want to get the full experience. But either way, most established FPS/RPG gamers should be fully able to enjoy this game, especially fans of strong narratives and intriguing atmospheres.

Replay value, to me, really makes a game worth your money.  As you may know, Bioshock is known to have different endings which rely on choices you make in the game.  There are multiple decisions you need to make throughout the game.  Some of those decisions are more difficult than the others.  To really get your money's worth out of this game, you should play to get every ending.  This will require many hours of game play, but each time you play it will seem like a brand new game.  There is also another game mode you can play called the 'Protector Trials'.  I am going to put this the best way I can.  Its hard.

In 2007, BioShock shook up the gaming world with its unique universe and exploration of dark philosophical themes. Two years later, [u]BioShock 2[/u] plunges us back into the fallen city of Rapture, but this time, with a new perspective: that of a Big Daddy, these imposing and terrifying protectors that we feared so much in the first opus. This game, developed by 2K Marin, offers a new story, new characters, and above all a new gameplay dynamic. But, does it manage to match the magic of its predecessor? Or is it simply an "encore" in troubled waters? Let's dive into this review and see if this second chapter succeeds in capturing the essence of Rapture.

[b]Good points[/b]
[u]Playing a Big Daddy:[/u] We play as Subject Delta, one of the first prototypes of Big Daddy. From the beginning, this perspective changes everything. You feel more powerful, but also more vulnerable than ever before. The combination of brute strength and agility gives you a new way to approach combat, with the iconic drill and the ability to use Plasmids alongside traditional weapons. Playing as a Big Daddy is both rewarding and nerve-wracking, as you find yourself in charge of a Little Sister, adding an emotional layer that the first game didn’t explore as deeply.

[u]Enhanced gameplay mechanics:[/u] Refines the gameplay of its predecessor with more fluid and dynamic combat. The ability to use Plasmids and weapons simultaneously makes for more intense and strategic encounters. Additionally, new weapons, such as the drill and harpoon launcher, are tailored to Big Daddy’s style and provide a brutal and satisfying combat experience. The sequel also features a more robust enemy variety, with foes like Brute Splicers and the terrifying Big Sisters providing a unique challenge and adding a constant level of danger.

[u]Introducing the Big Sisters:[/u] While the Big Daddies are protectors, the Big Sisters are their female counterparts—agile, aggressive, and downright fearsome. They appear to defend the Little Sisters you adopt or free, and each encounter with them is an intense ordeal. These fights are some of BioShock 2's most memorable moments, as the Big Sisters are fast, vicious, and unpredictable, forcing you to use all your skills and resources to survive.

[u]More emotional and touching story:[/u] Unlike the original BioShock, which dealt with philosophy in a more theoretical manner, BioShock 2 explores more emotional themes, including parenthood and sacrifice. Subject Delta is searching for Eleanor, his original Little Sister, in a quest for redemption and protection. The antagonist, Sofia Lamb, brings a vision that is the opposite of Andrew Ryan’s, advocating collectivism over individualism, which adds a new philosophical dimension to the story. This exploration of family ties and human nature offers an emotional depth that enriches the experience.

[u]Surprising and innovative multiplayer:[/u] Tried something bold: a multiplayer mode in the universe of Rapture. This mode, although often overlooked, is actually very well integrated. Set during the fall of Rapture, it allows players to take on the role of a citizen in the midst of despair, with epic PvP combat using Plasmids and iconic weapons. Although this multiplayer mode did not mark as much as the single player, it brings a touch of novelty and replayability.

[b]Bad points[/b]
[u]Less mysterious city of Rapture:[/u] One of the pleasures of BioShock was the discovery of Rapture, this place both fascinating and terrifying. In BioShock 2, this effect of discovery is less strong, because we are already familiar with the places and the atmosphere. Although the game introduces new areas, such as flooded districts and less explored sections of the city, the mystery has lost its luster. The nostalgia is still there, but for players of the first opus, this sequel does not offer the same wonder.

[u]Less complex and philosophical story:[/u] Although the story of BioShock 2 is touching, it is perceived as less rich in philosophical themes than the first. The story is more linear, with a clear motivation to find Eleanor and thwart Sofia Lamb's plans. The themes of Lamb's collectivism versus Ryan's individualism are less developed and less subtle than the ideals of freedom and power explored in the first game. This lack of philosophical depth may disappoint those expecting a new dose of existential musings.

[u]Little artistic innovation:[/u] Graphically, BioShock 2 takes up the style of the first game with a few minor improvements, but without any real artistic changes. While the technical quality is slightly better, the environments are relatively similar to those already explored, and the general aesthetic of Rapture remains unchanged. For those who were hoping for a marked visual evolution or more varied areas, the game can seem a little repetitive in terms of atmosphere.

[u]Sometimes frustrating AI:[/u] Enemy AI in BioShock 2 can be uneven. The Splicers, while terrifying in idea, sometimes act erratically or inconsistently, throwing themselves headlong into attacks or getting stuck in scenery. This unpredictability breaks the immersion a little and harms the fights that should be more tense. The Big Sisters, while formidable, can also show some AI weaknesses, especially if they get stuck on obstacles or don't always react logically.

[u]Redundancy in gameplay[/u] Like the first game, BioShock 2 follows a repetitive structure with exploration, combat, resource gathering, and skill upgrading sequences. The Little Sisters' quest can sometimes become mechanical: you fight a Big Daddy, adopt a Little Sister, and then protect her while she collects ADAM. While the concept is interesting, it can feel repetitive after a while, especially for players looking for variety in gameplay.

[b]Summary[/b]
[u]BioShock 2[/u] is a sequel that manages to deliver a satisfying experience without necessarily reaching the philosophical heights of its predecessor. With refined gameplay, more dynamic combat, and a touching narrative about family ties, the game explores a more emotional and intimate side of Rapture. Playing as a Big Daddy is a game changer, giving the player a sense of power while adding emotional vulnerability. While the discovery effect is less and the story is simpler, BioShock 2 is still a captivating adventure for those looking to extend their stay in Rapture.

The original [i]BioShock[/i] is a masterpiece of backstory and environmental design. It thrusts you into an evocative and cynical world, where every new area revels in discovery and delight.

The premise of [i]BioShock 2[/i] is that you're back in Rapture, [i]again[/i], though this time as a different character. Since [i]BioShock[/i]'s forte is in discovering its setting, reusing that setting in a sequel immediately limits its ability to surprise you. The result is that, though this is a full-length game, it conceptually feels like a DLC.

But that's not so bad in itself. It does feel great to be back in Rapture and the new character is fun to play. Unfortunately, the story is hard to follow. Perhaps more critically, it feels tacked-on. It doesn't seem like the world of [i]BioShock[/i] really needed this subplot. It does fill in one gap in the story of the first game, but it wasn't a particularly loose thread. That said, there is a sequence near the end of [i]BioShock 2[/i] that is quite surprising indeed. It's so awesome that it makes me wish there was more of it in the game as a whole.

Besides the story, this game is more combat-focused than its predecessor and in this respect it holds up pretty well. There are many power upgrades and weapons to mess around with and some of the enemies are pretty cool. It's all quite exciting for the most part, but in the latter third of the game it gets repetitive: same enemies, just more of them at once. There's even a DLC named [i]Protector Trials[/i], which is 100% combat. I skipped it because I had my fill in the main game.

Just don't skip the [i]Minerva's Den[/i] DLC, which is a side-story for what already feels like a side-story. And it's actually a better side-story than the main side-story. Am I making sense? In any case, it's worthy.

The bottom line is that if you've finished [i]BioShock[/i] and want more of its gameplay then [i]BioShock 2[/i] will deliver. Otherwise, it doesn't break new ground or significantly expand the [i]BioShock[/i] universe. Depending on your expectations, that might be pretty great.

BioShock 2, released in 2010 by 2K Games, had the difficult task of following up the legendary first game. While it doesn’t quite match the impact of the original, it expands on the lore, improves gameplay, and delivers an emotional, engaging experience.

Why BioShock 2 Deserves Recognition
🌊 A Fresh Perspective – Playing as a Big Daddy
Unlike the first game, where you were a vulnerable outsider, BioShock 2 puts you in the boots of Subject Delta—one of the earliest Big Daddies. This brings a new dynamic to combat and exploration, making you feel both powerful and vulnerable at the same time.

📖 A More Personal Story
While the first BioShock focused on political ideology and societal collapse, BioShock 2 tells a more emotional and character-driven story. The game revolves around your bond with Eleanor, the Little Sister you’re connected to, adding depth and emotional weight to your choices.

🔫 Enhanced Combat and Dual-Wielding
One of the biggest improvements is the ability to use Plasmids and weapons simultaneously, making combat faster, smoother, and more dynamic. Fighting off Splicers while setting traps, shocking enemies, and firing a shotgun feels incredibly satisfying.

🛠️ More Strategic Gameplay
🔹 Adopting Little Sisters – Instead of simply choosing to harvest or save them, you protect them while they gather ADAM, creating intense, wave-based encounters.
🔹 Big Sister Battles – These new enemies are agile, deadly, and terrifying, forcing you to be strategic with your resources.
🔹 More Varied Environments – Rapture feels more alive and detailed, with underwater sections that add new layers to exploration.

🎶 Haunting Soundtrack and Atmosphere
The art deco horror aesthetic of Rapture remains stunning and immersive, and the soundtrack continues to blend melancholic orchestral pieces with eerie 1950s-style music.

A Few Shortcomings
❌ Lacks the Original’s Groundbreaking Impact
Since BioShock 1 set such a high bar with its mind-blowing narrative and world-building, BioShock 2 feels more like an expansion than a revolutionary sequel.

❌ Multiplayer is Forgettable
While an interesting idea, the multiplayer mode felt unnecessary and wasn’t what made BioShock special.

Conclusion
BioShock 2 might not have the same iconic status as the first game, but it delivers a more refined, emotional, and immersive experience. With improved combat, a touching story, and deeper mechanics, it’s an essential play for fans of the series.

BioShock 2 is good.  Not exactly a surprise given the content of other available reviews on Steam, but why is it good seems the more important thing, something I'll try to address here.  I'm going to tell you why I think BioShock 2 is a worthy successor in the series.

First things first, to get right down to brass tacks BioShock 2 is a sequel, it is mostly more of the same gameplay (with a few twists) and the few innovations don't exactly break the bank in the inventiveness department.  A few new weapons and interesting plasmid variations and a small smattering of new enemy types don't do much to dispel the notion that the combat is totally more BiShock.  But that's not what makes a BioShock game, not really.  Sure, the combat has to be engaging enough to drive the narrative forward, but in this game it does that just enough.  No, much like the first, the true draw is the dark and twisted story, the narrative tapestry that shows the dark and twisted nature of those living in Rapture.

This game has you playing as a Big Daddy, the stalwart if myopic defenders of the Little Sisters.  In particular, you play a “prototype”, a nameless everyman changed into a monster but also a kind of father, and it is the theme of fatherhood that, like the first game, shares the roost with a political ideology to form the basis of the disastrous tale of the fall of Rapture.  Where the first game gazed on what genetics truly determine, on the pure unbridled force of Libertarianism and Capitalism, this game focuses on what it means to be a parent, and the equal sociopolitical dangers of a Communistic ideal that crosses the line into religious fervor.  It is the other side of the coin to Andrew Ryan's Rapture ideal of the individual's power in Rapture, the ideal of not just the social as one entity in a metaphorical manner, but what might happen if science could allow us all to actually become one.  And just as in the first game, the dangers of extremist politics show how such ideas can rip a society, and in particular a family apart.

This is the crux of the story: as the first game contained two father figures for the original protagonist, the Big Daddy is one of two parent figures presented in the game. Unlike before where you were being acted upon as a child with two parental figures, now you are one of the agents of change, and your actions effect the story in a more noticeable (if still superficial) manner.

It also drips the kind of scary, jarring atmosphere that is at once engaging to behold and terrifying to think about, the constructive and destructive nature of humankind.  Water drips, walls crack, but unlike before the underwater world outside Rapture is at least nominally explored, and it is beautiful, but sadly littered with the detritus of the once grand city.  The decay of the amazing city of Rapture is at once enthralling and disturbing, an emotional range that was demonstrated in BioShock, and is absolutely in full effect here.

To add to the positives Minerva's Den, a small DLC adventure contained within this game, is a wonderful look at how every last person in Rapture was hurt, changed, damaged by the vision of Andrew Ryan.  Rapture is a crucible and all it seems to produce is tragedy, and each game with it as it's setting allows us to see something of ourselves in it's tragedy.  

With arresting visuals, a story just as dark as it's sibling, and the upgraded combat engine, this game is well worth the time.  It is the other side of the coin, the “2” in this case being a quite literal extension of the first, and that is a very good thing indeed.

When it comes to Bioshock, the sequel has some really big daddy shoes to fill.

Story:

You play as Subject Delta, who is a big daddy. It's 1958 and you're patrolling Rapture with your little sister Eleanor. After Eleanor's mother Sofia Lamb takes Eleanor from Delta and then forces him to kill himself. Now it's 1968 and you awake from your ten year slumber and you set out to find Eleanor because if you don't you'll die. 

The story while decent, is nowhere near as good as the first Bioshock and at moments it can really slog. I think the pacing is all over the place as the game starts off incredibly slow, but once it sort of picks up it does get good, but never amazing. There's quite a few set pieces that almost border on being amazing, but there's that spark that the first game had that is just simply not here.

Graphics:

Bioshock 2 still looks great to this day and that will likely remain to be the case for a while. Rapture is still a brilliant location to explore and now a bit of time has passed and Rapture is now even more collapsed. Stopping and taking in the sights when inside Rapture and then even more amazing when you're outside walking around the sea floor. 

The enemy designs are again also really gnarly and the new additions of the Big Sisters who are tall thin and athletic Big Daddy type enemies are just absolutely awesome and top the first game. There are a few issues like a few of the textures being blurry and some minor texture pop ins, but these are so minor that I didn't really have a problem with them.

Audio:

Bioshock 2 again nails it's audio design. The soundtrack is again top notch with some really great music, that is about on par with what the composer created for the first Bioshock. It's great atmospheric music that really helps build this grand atmosphere when exploring Rapture and fighting enemies. 

The sound effects in my opinion are also better and really makes the first game look almost amateur (just barely). Since you play as a big daddy you have an access to a drill (more on it in the gameplay section), but honestly when that thing starts ripping into splicers and blood starts flying everywhere with the sounds it makes, it's just something incredibly satisfying about it.

Gameplay:

Bioshock 2 in the gameplay section is a bit of a mixed bag for me, in some ways I like it better than the first Bioshock, but in some ways it's even worse. First of all, for new players, Bioshock 2 is an explorational FPS game where your main goal is to go to point A to B while killing enemies, looking for upgrades for yourself and your weapons and of course looking for the notes and records that add more rich lore to the Rapture universe.

So let's start with the good. The combat in the first Bioshock could get really wonky at times, the aiming felt loose and sometimes the hit detection wouldn't be the best. However I feel like most of that is fixed in Bioshock 2 and the combat feels a lot tighter. It really feels good to wreak havoc with weapons and your arsenal is pretty big with stuff like rivet guns, shotguns and machine guns. Also Jack's trusty wrench is switched to a GOD DAMN DRILL and this thing feels great to use when ammo runs low, simply because it's satisfying to use, albeit in certain instances it's uses are limiting.

Another big change for the better is that allows you to use plasmid powers and weapons at the same time, which allows for tons of great combat possibilities, like freezing an enemy and then shattering them with your drill. It helps the combat flow much better and honestly makes it much more fun to get in combat scenarios. 

However there are a few negatives that really makes this game a major slog to get through. First thing is that there's a lot of times where you have to travel big distances back and forth if you intend to look for all the collectibles and honestly it does get slightly tedious in other longer chapters of the story. 

Also since you're a big daddy you have the ability to adopt little sisters and one of the major aspects is them collecting adam for you. Once you pick them a trail appears that leads you to a corpse and you have to protect them while they harvest the adam and these sections are so incredibly boring that I dread every time I have to do them. 

Verdict:

Bioshock 2 is nowhere near as good as the first game, but when it does shine, it shines bright. Even though the first few hours are slow, once the game gets going it does get really good and honestly it's just amazing exploring rapture as a big daddy. Not to mention now when you buy the game you also get the remastered version for free, which is a bonus. So definitely check it out if you're a fan of the first one.

Final Rating:
8/10

Pros:
+ New changes to combat are great
+ Playing as a Big Daddy is awesome
+ Graphics are still great
+ Amazing score

Cons:
- The first half of the game are insanely tedious
- The moments where you collect Adam are insanely boring
- Story doesn't have the same depth as the first game

[h1]BioShock 2 deserves more love[/h1]
Let me cut straight to the chase. 
Is BioShock 2 as memorable as BioShock? Perhaps not. 
Is the story as amazing? No. 
Is the story flawed in some senses? Yes. 
Is it a bad game? No, absolutely not. 

BioShock 2 is great in it's own right. It maintains most of the fantastic elements found in BioShock but (in my opinion) improves game-play in several ways.

[h1]Positive:[/h1]
- Still fantastically atmospheric
- Main story is OK [b]BUT[/b] the story in Minerva's Den (DLC) is incredible.
- Minerva's Den is really worth your time
- One plasmid and one weapon equipped at the same time. [b]YESSSSSSSSS![/b]
- Hacking system is greatly improved
- Hacking from a distance!
- Exploring is still as rewarding as ever - you'd be surprised how many places you can go
- BioShock 2 is challenging, especially fights with Big Daddies/Sisters

[h1]Negative:[/h1]
- Main story is not as memorable as BioShock

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
If you enjoyed BioShock I would urge you to give BioShock 2 a try too. Yes, the reviews are not as positive as they are for BioShock, but what really matters is your personal enjoyment of the game. I can say that I certainly enjoyed playing BioShock 2, and I think you would too.

Sequel 101: Take the original and make it bigger, better and more violent. Bioshock 2 covers its bases well with expanded gameplay, stage design and enemy variation. The story lacks the surprise twist from the original, but it makes up for it in buckets by simply being a better game. 

The original Bioshock was a surprise hit from 2007. It offered incredible atmosphere, a riveting story and entertaining gameplay. All the ingredients for an instant classic. The sequel had a lot to live up and it took a slightly different approach. Incredible atmosphere, an entertaining story and literally riveting gameplay. For the sequel you get to play as a big daddy, the huge lumbering divers on the game’s cover. Arguably the most intelligent design choice for a sequel since Terminator 2. 

Bioshock 2 is an insane power fantasy. You play as an armoured badass in the run down districts of the once shining city of Rapture. You are subject Delta, an old cover model and you are called back from the beyond to rescue your daughter from some head-shrink. Yeah, the story is a bit thin, but your motivation is clear: Save your daughter from a psycho and kill, murder and maim anyone who gets in your way. 

Playing as the big poppa gives you access to the iconic drill, a rivet gun (earlier pun intended), a huge machine gun, an elephant gun that has no business being fired from the hip, a spear gun taken from the bow of a whaler and a rocket launcher that probably fell of an armoured truck. In your other hand you command the forces of nature to shock, roast and freeze your enemies. You are a one man army and you are not going to let anyone get in your way. 
To compensate, the enemies are more numerous and aggressive. You’ll often fight against dozens while also hacking and setting traps at the same time. You’ll also brave gauntlets against an incoming tide of enemies while you defend your little sister helper while she’s gathering valuable power-up juice. The addition of these standoffs is a welcome one and adds some serious meat to the gameplay. Setting traps allows for some really creative tricks. This goes on from start to finish and gets more intense along the way. No difficulty falloff here. 
Difficulty in general; Bioshock 2 is quite challenging in its own right. Enemies hit hard and never stop attacking. So even on normal does it present a good challenge (unlike Infinite’s 1999 mode, which was as easy as shooting fish in a barrel.) Furthermore, the city of Rapture looks just as gorgeous as before. Ok, maybe the textures are a bit washed out, but when the place is flooded, everything looks washed out. 

One major problem persists the game and that is the stability. Bioshock 2 has a nasty habit of crashing to desktop for no apparent reason. I’m still vexed as to why it happens, but it annoys the living hell out of me and it has me save every ten minutes to prevent losing all that progress. Also, the controls are somewhat of a mess. You’ll have to tinker with them, but its manageable. There’s also a multiplayer mode…which I’m not even touching. I came here to drill people and save little sisters; and that’s just what this game lets you do.
I wonder how many irrelevant games are coming back, with reboots, remakes, and BioShock still on hold. Is it really over?

BioShock 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed by 2K Marin and published by 2K Games.

In a game you step into the shoes of Big Daddy known as Subject Delta. His patrol on 1958 New Year's Eve ends up with a bang-literally, as he gets shot and killed while his Little Sister gets taken away. 
A decade later he gets revived with a goal of finding his Sister, or he will die. Delta without much of a choice ventures through once beautiful, now ruined by civil war underwater city Rapture. 

Gameplay wise it's same as first game with additional tasks related to Little Sister coming from Big Daddy role. So once again you will wander through Rapture location by location and complete a set of objectives in each. Locations are usually non-linear and encourage exploration to find better items, similar to BioShock 1. However unlike first title, you cannot return to previous locations you have visited so be sure to check everything twice before going further.
While you explore you face off different types of enemies, from splicers and security systems to Big Daddies wandering around.
Combat works in the same way as previously, to eliminate your enemies you have a wide variety of weapons, including a melee drill and ranged firearms, plasmids allowing you to set enemies on fire or control them if you have enough eve, and enviroment to use. Enemies drop useful items, including money you can spend at vending machines, food or drinks that restore your health/eve bars, and ammo.

ADAM continues to play an important role in upgrading your character. If you want to increase amount of health you have, unlock new tonic slots or get yourself new, powerful versions of plasmids, you need adam. To earn it you have to find Little Sisters and kill their Big Daddies. Here comes a new element of gameplay, as now besides usual choice of rescuing/harvesting Little Sisters, you can scavenge for dead bodies and protect her while she collects adam from them, giving you more of it to spend.
Besides plasmids and normal upgrades, you have tonics-passive buffs which affect a variety of gameplay elements. Some make hacking easier, some make you tougher, and some simply make items cheaper. You find them spread across the city and at shops, with main change being lack of limitation. While in first game you could use a specific amount of tonics per different mechanic to not unbalance things, there are no restrictions here.
Hacking returns and now with new tool you can hack different machines on long range making things way easier, allowing you to set up traps for unsuspicious enemies, if you will beat a minigame that is.
And since you play as Big Daddy with powerful arsenal, stealth which you would-could use in first title here is basically completly removed and game encourages you to play agressive.
Besides stealth devs dropped pointless crafting system from BioShock 1.
In short, gameplay plays out in a same way like previous title, with addition of protection but with removal of stealth and crafting.

Narration was one of the most crucial elements of first title and here it's still strong. Themes slightly changed, with new antagonist in the main seat game asks crucial questions on what went wrong with Rapture and why it was doomed to fail, combining both social and utopian topics for you to think about while scavenging and trying to survive.
Unfortunately characters are not as good as in first title, main villain is good but rest of the characters is average, mainly they show up on one level and never come back or have a very little screentime. 

Main problem with BioShock 2 is simply lack of new elements nor innovations in gameplay, so game feels repetitive, especially if you played first one fairly recently. Not a bad gameplay of course, it's still a very enjoyable game to play buuut you wish to do something new and fresh once in a while instead of same exploration/combat/hacking.

Bioshock 2 features a story-driven Multiplayer called "Fall of Rapture". It takes place during a civil war in 1959 and you play as one of citizens who just tried out first plasmid and now joins one of the factions. It features a variety of gamemodes, from basic Deathmatch to Capture the Sister, each has "free for all" and "team" option, with weapons and locations from first title. There is also a partial customization and progression system! 
Pretty fun but very dead nowdays, it's almost impossible to find a game. 

Performance wise game works smoothly, besides that one late game moment where textures cause a crash and you have to drop their quality to medium in order to progress. 

Just like previous title BioShock 2 features beautful soundtrack fitting thematically to the setting. Voice acting and sound effects are top notch. It's a shame there is a weird issue with gunshots as while firing sound cuts in and out so you hear some shots and some you don't.

BioShock 2 follows the footsteps of a first game with same gameplay plus setting and while lack of new elements is problematic, it's still a superb title. 9/10.

The first Bioshock is a great game, but it isn’t perfect. It suffers from odd level design and a messy final act. But despite its short development time, Bioshock 2 takes everything great about the first game and streamlines it. Gone are the old PC-era RPG elements and bullet-spongy bosses. The way research works in this game promotes more variety in gunplay, pushing players to try plasmid and weapon combos they might normally not. This makes 2 extremely replayable.

The story here elaborates on a small but important part of Bioshock: the Big Daddies and Little Sisters. Putting you in the shoes of an “old-school” Daddy that supposedly existed before the events of the first game, Delta somehow manages to help us feel so much more than Jack ever did.

Our relationship with Eleanor is moving and organic. Lamb feels like a great successor villain-wise to the loud and proud Ryan. Bioshock 2's story is weirdly similar to Neon Genesis Evangelion, but with a Socialism-fearing American twist. Through themes of fatherhood battling unrighteous use of equality and unity, our actions feel much more fleshed out than the black-and-white “choice” in Bioshock (which is ironic considering that game’s main message). This game makes your choices feel like they really matter.

2 abandons a plot twist and a final boss to focus more on its spectrum of endings, which feel natural based on our choices and their influence. If Delta is good, Eleanor becomes good. If Delta is evil, Eleanor becomes evil. If Delta made mixed/nonsensical choices, Eleanor becomes broken and confused. This is especially great with how thought-provoking some of the choices are: like does Gil deserve to live, or should he be mercy-killed as he previously asked? Not to forget the Mark Meltzer subplot, which is its own whole fascinating journey that was originally revealed through an ARG before 2 released.

The multiplayer is pretty great despite how often people cite it as feeling "tacked on." Clearly a decent amount of love was put into it, even if it is unbalanced (all you need is Electro Bolt and the damage-upgraded crossbow).

This was my first Bioshock game, but I think even if I had played the first game first, I’d know that this is the better game. And probably the greatest shooter of all time. "Love is just a chemical, we give it meaning by choice." Wild that some people think this story is weaker...

"Would I recommend this game" is a difficult question. The game itself is good. It may be the weakest installment in the Bioshock franchise to date, but the weakest installment of an amazing series is still pretty great. The reason I decided to say "no" is because of the amount of crap I had to go through just to get the game to play. I have about 16 hours of playtime logged, and I'm willing to bet a good half of it was spent troubleshooting, checking to see if various fixes worked, replaying segments and sometimes entire levels... it got old, fast. For a game that's been out for so long to not have a single fix for everything is pretty inexcusable, especially one that you're expected to pay for. I ended up looking up various guides on Steam and 2K's support forum to get the game to work, uninstalling and reinstalling the game twice, uninstalling and reinstalling programs on my computer, tinkering with files, settings, and compatibility modes, even editing the .ini file itself. The most prominent issues I had were it constantly crashing shortly after starting the game (just when you get the rivet gun), on the loading screen to Siren Alley, the loading screen for Fontaine Futuristics, and near the end of the Fontaine Futuristics level. All of these required multiple attempts on my part to fix and finally finish.

On the other hand, my closest friend also has the Steam version of this game and reports not having the same problems. But for any game to give anyone this much problem, I wouldn't recommend spending your money on a roll of the dice to see whether or not it'll work (for the record, I had no problems with the original Bioshock, so don't assume that just because you played through that with no problems, you won't encounter issues here). It's truly upsetting that what could, and should, have been a pleasant, fun gaming experience turned into a frustrating nightmare, and as soon as I got to the ending, I uninstalled and washed my hands of it. Multiplayer? Other endings? Achievements? Forget about it, not worth the grief.

If you do decide to give it a shot (in which case I recommend a console version), here's what I thought, issues getting the game to run aside: like I said, it may be the weakest link in Bioshock's Great Chain, but that doesn't mean it's a total waste of time. A lot of the gameplay was simplified from the first game (such as hacking, researching, even the Tonics all being in one area instead of being in four categories with different slots you need to open), some undoubtedly for the better (it's telling hacking and researching didn't appear in Infinite) and some for the worst. There is the mechanic of carrying around Little Sisters and guarding them as they gather, akin to the ending of the first game only much faster and less frustrating (with tonics to maximize ADAM and speed up the process becoming available fairly early). However, there's up to three Little Sisters per level, and each one can gather up to twice. It's really up to you how you decides to handle them, as in the original, but the fact remains you're still going to have to throw down with a Big Daddy and you're still going to have to deal with them somehow if you want ADAM.

The main point that this game got a lot of flack for was the story. The game was, admittedly, a cash grab/attempt to keep the Bioshock name alive while Ken Levine and Take-Two/Irrational were working on Infinite, farmed out to 2K Marin. I, personally, think they did a decent enough job with what they had. The story lacked the symbolism and social commentary that made the first one so powerful, and a lot of the mystique and creepiness that Rapture had during the first outing is absent here. I won't even claim the story made total sense in the end (you pretty much need all the supplemental materials, including the dubiously canon novel Bioshock: Rapture by John Shirley, which did have input from Ken Levine, to make it close to solid). And, to quote the venerable Yahtzee, the original Bioshock's story didn't really need a direct sequel. But I wouldn't say the whole thing is a wash, either. For one thing, there's at least two moments in this game (I won't give spoilers) that I personally felt were some of the most powerful in the entire series to date.

It really seems like when they were at the drawing board, whether intentionally or not, 2K Marin got it in their head that in making a game that wasn't basically an exact rehash of the first, they needed to make it as different as possible, and ended up creating the original on Opposite Day. WHAT FOLLOWS ARE SPOILERS FOR THE FIRST GAME!

Whereas in Bioshock, you play a man that starts out with nothing and gradually finds his purpose throughout the game, in Biooshock 2, the main character has lost everything, including his identity (he's a Big Daddy), and is on a desperate journey, whether out of compulsion or genuine concern, to reclaim the one thing he had left. Whereas Andrew Ryan was a staunch objectivist who constantly extolled the value of looking out for yourself and acting in your own self-interest, the main villain of this game, Sofia Lamb, is a collectivist, with a cult built around being utterly selfless and willing to lay down your life if it would better serve mankind as a whole. Throughout the first game, you're guided by a man who seems kind, helpful, and sincere, but ultimately betrays you and reveals you were an unwitting pawn in his grand plan all along. In Bioshock 2, you're largely guided by a man who is a confessed and mostly unrepentant sleezeball, who makes no secret of the fact that he's mostly using you as a means to get him out of Rapture as well so he can profit off of the technology there. As he knows his plans hinge on you achieving your goal, he's willing to play ball. And let me add that 2K Marin deserves some major props for making a character that is so slimy, yet ultimately charming and likable.

All in all, it's a fun game. You won't miss anything for skipping it, especially now that Infinite is out, and I personally wouldn't blame you if you decided to give it a pass and not bother with this slightly subpar installment in the franchise. But with 2K Marin now in charge of the franchise as a whole, it might be worth it if you're a fan of the series just to see how they've handled it in the past. Just, for the love of little yellow duckies, play it on a console and don't waste your time, money, and possibly hours of frustration trying to play the Steam version.

BioShock 2, the very definition of a misunderstood sequel!

And so here I was, about 4 years after I played the original BioShock for the first time (the one on steam was the second) and was left amazed by the marvellously haunting underwater world and history of Rapture, the time had come to see how the story moved on.

Truth be told, I am by nature negatively biased towards sequels of great games, since the result rarely is on par with the originals.
At the same time, from online reviews and friends opinions I was expecting a generally mediοcre sequel, not really bad, but a lot inferior.

What I got instead was a great game that was a lot reminiscent of its predecessor and that at the same time managed to put it's own touch and distinguish itself from it!

The game is vastly big, since, except from its main single player story, which is already long enough to be comparable to the first one's, it also includes a multiplayer campaign, plus two more DLCs, so let me analyze them one by one!

- The single player campaign, for starters: you start out as a Big Daddy (an older model of it actually), with it's two trademark weapons (the drill and the rivet gun) and the ability to escort Little Sisters at their ADAM gatherings, which I found to be a really nice idea to stand out from the first game, since it gave you the opportunity to see the world from a different perspective.

The story is a bit confusing at first, you don't know who you are and what you are doing and I'll admit that, while I initially liked that, as the game progressed on this "amnesia" of sorts got a bit tiresome, since it prevented you from enjoying the story and its (small) twists.

The first game was ahead in that aspect, since it made you start out pretty much confident about who you were and what you were doing, only to destroy that all at its half, with an amazing twist, one of the best of its kind. However the remaining half of the original BioShock wasn't as thrilling as the first one, though it definitely wasn't bad, just decent.

Now, BioShock 2 took another route, to the end of the game you get to know very few things about the protagonist, as, little by little, you learn something more, all until the final levels, where the big twist kicks in and you find all the truth about yourself! The twist was, maybe, just a little inferior from the one of the first game, but it was still very good.

Continuing on, aside from the story, the game made some great additions in the gameplay, that improved a lot the old one. For starters, the weapons/plasmids system was positively changed a bit, making them easier to handle, while at the same time new weapons and plasmids were added, greatly differentiating themselves from the older ones.

Speaking of gameplay, when I first played Dishonored (another great game) I remember describing it as a "stealth based BioShock", well... upon playing BioShock 2 I found even more similarities to Dishonored than the first game and not just in gameplay, but storywise too (ie, in Dishonored you have to save a little girl named Emily and in BioShock 2 one named Eleanor). After all, Arkane Studios was involved in the making of both games, so that probably played its part. However, there too, Dishonored took it's own distinctive path, so I wouldn't call it a ripoff, in fact it even improved on many of these similarities that I noticed between said games (like a fast teleporting plasmid present in BioShock 2's multiplayer, named Aerodash, which was a lot similar to the vastly superior Blink ability in Dishonored... and how much I missed that ability in BioShock 2... ).

Moving on, aside from the improved weapon and plasmid mechanics and some new splicers, BioShock 2 introduced an amazing foe: the Big Sister, who essentially was an evolution of the Big Daddy! I found them great for a change in the game's world, since they were really tough to beat and getting ready to "greet" them was scary enough, sometimes (I even remember getting ready to fight one and getting my ass kicked, only to be saved by, not one, but two cluelessly walking Big Daddies, that, upon being caught in the Big Sister's attacks, started attacking her as well, saving my lucky self!).

Another big change in the gameplay was the ability to "wirelessly" hack machines, a change which I ended up really appreciating, despite the hack being done in real time, with enemies potentially attacking you.

The graphics and soundtrack were, more or less, similar to the first's, with the former being slighly improved, but nothing too great. In itself that was a good thing, since it made the game stay closer to its predecessor.
The game's levels dimensions were also changed, since the first game had many levels split in two parts (maybe because of limitations PCs had at that time), while BioShock 2 had 9 huge levels, which I mistakenly thought to be few at first, though being slightly smaller in total.

Lastly, the game's main antagonist wasn't as thrilling as the two ones of the original BioShock, but she was good enough.
Thankfully the final levels, upon learning your true identity and onwards, were quite good and action packed, so much that they even provided you with a great ally, which I won't spoil and I'll let you discover for yourself (for a single level you also got to play as a Little Sister, which was cool)!
The ending was, once again, faithful to the original, where some of your choices in the game affected its outcome (much like in Dishonored, too).

- Changing subject, I'll now go to the multiplayer campaign: overall, I didn't feel satisfied by it and that being because the game had some, difficult enough, multiplayer achievements, while at the same time it was not optimized well enough, resulting in a lot of lag (myself aside, I found others having the same problem too) and in almost empty lobbies, making the achievement hunt quite frustrating.

However, that said, the multiplayer part was not all bad, it's gameplay was in fact quite good and balanced (though not entertaining enough) and it took part in a period before the events of the first BioShock, during Rapture's civil war, making it a bit more interesting.

- And to the final part, we get to the game's two DLCs: the Protector Trials and Minerva's Den.

The first one was not much related to the main story, but not totally unrelated too. 
Once again reminding me of Dishonored's first DLC (Dunwall City Trials), it comprised of many challenges were you once again assumed the role of a Big Daddy and had to protect a Little Sister during her ADAM gatherings, but with a specific set of weapons and plasmids each time, making the whole thing fun enough, while mixing just a bit of story in it and awarding you with some extra art and trailers of BioShock 2, for every succesful gathering you made.

The second DLC was, instead, a continuation of the story and ended up being really good and long just enough to keep your interest on. You once again took the role of a Big Daddy with a mysterious story on its back, immersing yourself in the game's levels to find it out, all of this happening in another, unexplored, part of Rapture, with new weapons and enemies mixed in (the Ion Laser gun being its coolest addition).
The DLC's ending was good enough, with the final twist being slightly more predictable than the main game's, but not too much, while at the same time providing a good closure to the world of Rapture.

All in all, I found BioShock 2 to be a fantastic game and only slightly inferior to the original, most of it being due to the fact that you were already introduced and familiar to the world of Rapture from the latter. Hopefully the third game, BioShock Infinite, will manage to reignite the marvel of discovering a hidden city, this time in the sky (can't wait to play it as well)!

One of my favorite games ever. [b]While not as philosophical as Bioshock 1, I can't help but feel completely immersed in the role of a Big Daddy[/b]. The way you move, slow and heavy, the helmet UI, the gun types you use, the drill-dash move, the gathering sections with Little Sisters, while they piggyback on you and comment on kills you make, it all adds up to a wonderful experience, in my opinion. Of course, the Rapture setting complements all that. It's a fine game, and I'm too biased to comment any further.

This review is based on 100% completion and 38.8 hours of gameplay.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? No – and that’s purely because of the technical performance issues I experienced on PC. These problems had a major impact on my experience, which is really unfortunate because the game itself is one of my all-time favourites. I’ve 100% completed it multiple times on console and again on the remastered version, but this PC port of the original is rough. Unless you’re willing to troubleshoot, I can’t recommend buying it on its own.

When I first launched the campaign, I was hit with constant crashes. It was genuinely unplayable at first. I eventually managed to stabilise it by following a combination of community fixes – specifically [b][i][url= https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319446016] Ghost’s [/url][/i][/b] guide and [b][i][url= https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=210917941] DENIS_Biomechanoid 🍑 [/url][/i][/b] guide. One required editing .ini values, and the other involved downloading additional files. It didn’t eliminate the crashes entirely, but it made the game stable enough for me to finish. I’ve left a detailed comment on Ghost’s guide explaining what worked for me, so if you run into the same problems, I’d suggest checking that first.

The frustrating part is that none of this should be necessary. No game you purchase should require this level of tweaking just to function properly. Interestingly, the multiplayer ran fine for me for around the 19 hours I was in it. The issues were strictly tied to the single-player campaign.

There were also smaller annoyances – full screen could behave oddly, tabbing out sometimes caused problems, and settings would occasionally reset themselves. It just isn’t a well-optimised PC port. If not for these issues, I would recommend this game without hesitation.

Putting the technical issues aside though, the game itself is fantastic.

Narratively, it’s dark, gritty and keeps you hooked from start to finish. Exploring Rapture as a Big Daddy is a brilliant twist, and while the structure is mostly linear, your choices do influence certain outcomes and endings. The writing fits the world perfectly and keeps you immersed throughout.

Visually, it has held up well for its age. Yes, it looks dated compared to modern titles, but the art direction and world design are still strong. The environmental storytelling, paired with the audio logs scattered throughout, adds real depth to Rapture and makes it feel alive.

The sound design is just as good. Hearing splicers in the distance, the heavy footsteps of Big Daddies, and the eerie voices of the Little Sisters all build tension constantly. Everything works together to create a compelling atmosphere.

Gameplay-wise, it’s simple and works exactly as intended – when the game itself behaves. There’s a good variety of weapons and plasmids to use and upgrade. It’s not just run-and-gun either; you have defence-style segments, boss encounters, search-and-retrieve objectives and more. The variety helps keep things fresh rather than relying on one single gameplay loop throughout.

Multiplayer exists in this original version but was removed from the remastered edition. There are still small pockets of players active, but from my experience the remaining community can be quite toxic and mostly look to steamroll new players. I wouldn’t recommend jumping into it casually. The single-player campaign is the real highlight here.

There is DLC, most notably Minerva’s Den, which I genuinely enjoyed. It adds a strong self-contained story, new weapons, new enemies and new areas, all of which are well designed and worth playing. The Protector Trials mode, however, didn’t do much for me. It’s essentially a series of challenge arenas where you protect a Little Sister using pre-determined loadouts. I found it tedious rather than fun. Personally, I think they could have just stuck with Minerva’s Den.

Overall, I love this game itself. But the technical issues I experienced on PC are simply too significant for me to recommend buying it standalone. I purchased it as part of the [i]BioShock: The Collection bundle[/i], which includes the other games, and that’s the route I’d suggest. The bundle goes on sale regularly, and that’s the best way to pick this up – not on its own.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
[b][i]DLC is required for 100% completion, and there are also 15 multiplayer achievements. Because of that, a boosting group of at least four people is highly recommended.[/i][/b]

Overall, the achievements are fairly straightforward, and there are plenty of guides online since the game is quite old now. I’d strongly suggest using the roadmap on TrueAchievements, as it gives a good structure to follow.

The multiplayer achievements aren’t too bad in terms of requirements – the main issue is that the multiplayer is basically dead, and progress cannot be fully unlocked in private matches. You can make progress on some achievements in private games [i](for example, reaching level 40)[/i], but you will still need to play a public match afterwards for the achievements to actually pop. There’s a guide by [b][i][url= https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=481757730] Murphy’s Lawyer [/url][/i][/b] on Steam that goes over this in more detail.

One thing to be aware of: some people have had trouble getting the map-related achievements to unlock. A few players have reported that these need to be done within a single game session – meaning you can’t do all maps privately, close the game, and then come back the next day expecting it to unlock after one public match. Instead, you need to play the private matches and then immediately go into a public match while the game is still running. It doesn’t affect everyone, but worth noting just in case. 

Also, the map-specific achievements each have their own condition, even if you did all the private matches correctly:
[list]
    [*][b]Man About Town[/b] – Played at least one non-private match on each multiplayer map. → Should unlock without trouble as long as all maps have been played in private beforehand.
    [*][b]Aqua Incognita[/b] – Played at least one non-private match on each downloadable content map. → Must be a DLC map – it won’t pop on a standard map. [i](I only needed one DLC public match for this.)[/i]
    [*][b]Territorial[/b] – Won a non-private match in each of the 6 new maps. → You must win – either a team mode or free-for-all should count. Using the TIE method works as well, however some players may need to win one extra match on any of the needed maps afterwards for it to unlock properly. For more details, see the comments on TrueAchievements for this achievement.
[/list]
When boosting, you need a minimum of 4 players to start a public lobby. The main issue you’ll face is randoms joining and griefing your progress. There’s still a tiny number of players active who will try to ruin what you’re doing – even if you ask nicely – so be prepared. The best ways to deal with that are:[list]
    [*]Get enough achievement hunters to fill the lobby [i](I believe that’s 10 players)[/i], or
    [*]If a random joins, work together to eliminate them until they leave
[/list]
For example, when we were doing Adam Grab and attempting a tied match [i](nobody touches the Little Sister for 10 minutes)[/i], we’d all protect her – and if a random showed up, we made them the main target until they rage-quit. It’s not pretty, but sometimes you have to adapt when others are actively trying to ruin your session.

Aside from the multiplayer achievements, everything else is easily done solo and offline besides the technical issues with the game itself.

[H1] TLDR: 9/10 Basically a Streamlined Bioshock 1 With a Slightly Worse but Still Really Great Story. Nails Expanding the World of Rapture [/H1]

[h3] Actual Review (Censored Spoilers) [/h3]
Where to begin? This game does so much right in refining the Bioshock experience coming off of BS1. I didn't have a single crash or lag spike the entire playthrough like a lot of people are mentioning. Irrational Games handled [spoiler] playing as a Big Daddy [/spoiler] significantly better in this game than in BS1. The difference of weight, power, size, and speed really helps separate BS2's gameplay from the first. As a matter of fact I'll dive into that right now.

[h3] The Gameplay is Nearly Perfect...But... [/h3]
The gameplay has been streamlined and optimized to near perfection compared to BS1's in my opinion, however let's get the negatives out of the way first. On its own, the way BS2 is structured makes certain things suffer in terms of gameplay, but the combat itself I think is better than BS1's. What do I mean by that? Well, There's some elements that are a step back from what BS1 did, and the overall gameplay suffers because of that. For example you cannot travel back to previous areas like in BS1, which is a story-tied decision not a gameplay one. You also don't have as much of a focus on tonic building, because you can equip a much larger amount of tonics than in BS1. Meaning you can just kinda have a cover-all setup that does most everything you want anyway, which hurts the depth of the combat. Lastly (and this isn't really a negative, but just a shift in the direction of the combat design for story related reasons) this game has a lot of defense sections. Now I didn't mind most of them, they're this game's biggest chance for you to test your knowledge and optimize your tactics. You might love it or hate it but regardless of that this game is completely geared toward planning out your moves before striking. Play your cards right and you'll find this game is a breeze even on hard.

Okay so with the negatives cleared, on to the positives, which EASILY overshadow literally everything I just talked about. The combat of this game is tuned so finely it's almost scary. By far the single best change is that hacking isn't terrible anymore. The gameplay halting, slow af flow puzzle hacking of BS1 was the single worst element of the entire game by an extremely large margin. Gone is that entire system, and in comes a simple horizontal bar at the bottom of the screen with a needle moving back and forth. Time still moves as you hack, and it's a simple game of place the needle in the green. You don't need a bunch of tonics hogging space to make hacking easier either, just a couple simple hacking buffs. The second best change BS2 makes is making the camera less annoying to use. Instead of pictures that are graded, it's a film reel that you roll before combat which is then graded upon killing the enemy, this makes maxing out enemy research way faster and easier to do, which is necessary since you can't backtrack. Other changes include making weapons less redundant, meaning no more pistol that you use in the first few areas and then never use again once you get the machine gun/crossbow. You also switch ammo types WAY faster, instead of doing the entire reload animation every single time. Speaking of ammo types, They’re a lot more interesting in this game. Instead of the basic, piercing, and antipersonnel types that a lot of weapons share, every weapon has its own ammo types. The original 3 types are used for the machine gun and that's it. Tons of weapons allow you to use them for both trapping and direct damage, including the first gun you get, which you’ll be continually using the entire game unlike BS1’s pistol.

Now onto enemies. Most splicers have been made visually distinct from each other this time around, with enemies like the spider splicers actually looking different than normal splicers. Big Daddies also have been given subclasses instead of just visual differences. Combat is a constant battle of learning what weapons and plasmids work for what enemy, which is great because no two enemies have the exact same weaknesses. As far as their visual appearances, enemies and especially splicers don’t blend into the background nearly as often unless they’re intended to do so, which was an issue I had with BS1’s splicers and that game’s overall visual design. Speaking of which….

BS2 fixes pretty much every visual issue I had with BS1. I had serious eye strain and headache issues playing BS1 for several reasons, and thankfully the higher texture and geometry quality and improved/different lighting design has eliminated almost all of those problems. Of course you still have the low FOV which can still be changed by adding a hotkey, but overall I barely had any eye strain except a few small enclosed sections.

[h3] Story [/h3]
Storywise it's almost as interesting as the original game's, and it thankfully doesn't copy that story's formula. I say it's less compelling for one main reason: There's quite a few characters that seem to only serve the purpose of delivering exposition and allow you to move to the next location. [spoiler] Specifically Sinclair and Eleanor, who have either little chance to develop much character, or their character is ruined by not shutting up with "go here and do this' dialogue/story exposition. [/spoiler] This game would have a lot of chill exploration moments if characters would just stop talking and let you advance the plot on your own without them telling you how and where to do it. Other than that the plot itself is pretty solid. The worldbuilding is on par if not better than BS1, and it has a lot of psychological deep dives into Rapture as a concept and it's citizens.

[h3] DLC & Achievements [/h3]
The Minerva's Den and the Protector Trails DLC are also just as fun as the main campaign. The story of Minerva's Den is super interesting and loosely follows the twist structure that BS1 has, which definitely works better in this much shorter  playthrough than if it was done in the main story. It adds a few new elements and weapons, and a few achievements as well. As for the protector trails, they're kind of grindy, but they really made me appreciate the defense section design this game has as a core concept and it made me much more creative in my gameplay with the limited gear selection each trail has. Compared to my main game playthrough, where I kind of just used the same tactics for each defense section.

Lastly I want to mesh together the achievement hunting and multiplayer into one section. Right off the bat I wish the multiplayer was a success and still had an active playerbase. It has so many fun gameplay loops and a good progression system with a focus on character builds just like singleplayer does.
